background.definition: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is composed of a group of hereditary disorders in which progressive cellular dysfunction and loss leads to eventual retinal atrophy and vision loss. Genotypic and phenotypic variability is considerable.

list.listitem: The worldwide prevalence of RP is approximately 1 in 4000.
In the state of Maine, the incidence of RP is approximately 1 in 3500.
A study in Israel found a prevalence of 1 in 2400 individuals.
RP affects approximately 1 million persons worldwide.

Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked recessive forms have been described. Mitochondrial and digenic mutations have been reported. A single pedigree is suggestive of possible Y-linked disease.

The most common cause of autosomal dominant RP in the United States is rhodopsin Pro23His, creating a mutation in rhodopsin, a photopigment in rod outer segments. Pro347Leu is the next most common mutation.
Early in the disease, there is a shortening of rod outer segments, which eventually leads to cell loss via apoptosis. This is usually seen in midperiphery. Cones undergo a similar process.
Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells detached from the underlying Bruch's membrane and migrate into retinal tissue surrounding the blood vessels (seen clinically as bone spicules).
RPE migration, along with possible diminished metabolic need, may lead to vascular attenuation.
Retinitis pigmentosa GTPase regulator-associated X-linked retinitis pigmentosa is a rare and more severe form with 3% to 8% visual loss per year over time.
Family members of a patient with RP should undergo ophthalmologic examinations. C
Symptoms and signs of RP include nyctalopia, flashing lights, and clumsiness at night. C
Key clinical findings on ophthalmologic examination include waxy pallor of the optic nerve, retinal vascular attenuation, and retinal pigmentary changes (bone spicules). C
Patients need a full ophthalmologic examination with dilation that may include visual field and electroretinogram (ERG) tests. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Optic nerve and retinal vasculature are usually normal
Pigment clumps rather than bone spicules
Pigmentary changes follow course of retinal veins; ERG normal or minimally abnormal
History of thioridazine, chlorpromazine, antimalarial, and quinine use; pigment changes variable
Unilateral; may see encased nematode within retina; ERG abnormal in affected eye only

list.listitem: Symptoms include nyctalopia (easily disoriented compared with others in dim settings; accident prone, particularly at night [do not confuse nyctalopia with blurry vision at night]), clumsiness in low-light conditions, and flashing lights. Some patients are asymptomatic.
In patients with RP, central vision may be normal or diminished; peripheral vision may be reduced; color vision may be normal or consistent with tritanopia (blue-vision loss).

Anterior segment findings include cataracts, keratoconus, myopia, and astigmatism. Posterior segment findings include vitreous pigment cell, waxy pallor of optic nerve, bone spicules in peripheral retina, retinal vascular attenuation, and cystoid macular edema.
Dilated ophthalmoscopy may reveal classic findings of waxy pallor of the optic nerve, attenuated retinal vasculature, and retinal pigmentary changes (bone spicules).
Formal visual field testing using automated perimetry may reveal constriction of the visual field, which is not diagnostic, but may be used to follow disease progression.
Full-field ERG typically mirrors the visual field loss, but may be normal to extinguished, and varies depending on the type of RP. It may be used to follow disease progression.
Multifocal ERG may be used to follow disease progression and assess central retinal function.
Genetic testing/counseling may be helpful to determine the specific variant.
Elicit symptoms of headache, restricted visual fields, flashing lights, and nyctalopia. Ask about family history of eye conditions and aforementioned symptom complex.
Order a full ophthalmologic evaluation, including visual field and ERG testing.
Consider genetic testing.
Give high-dose vitamin A (15,000 IU/day) under medical supervision. B
Avoid vitamin E supplementation. B
Retinal implant is an option for selected patients. B

Oral lutein supplementation (20 mg/day) for 6 months increased macular pigment but not visual acuity in patients with RP. A second small study found improvement in visual field, and possibly a small improvement in visual acuity, using a 30 mg per day dosage.
Docosahexaenoic acid supplementation may preserve cone ERG responses in X-linked RP; larger trials are needed to confirm.
Vitamin A alone and combined vitamin A and vitamin E supplementation are currently being studied by the National Eye Institute.
Intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) are sometimes recommended, primarily based on case series and case reports. However, there have been no clinical trials.
An uncontrolled Phase 1 trial found some improvements in visual acuity with oral N-acetylcysteine, but randomized trials are needed to assess efficacy as well as safety.
Limited evidence found no benefit of oral minocycline on progression of visual loss.
A randomized trial with 70 patients found no overall benefit of oral branched-chain amino acids.
Fetal retinal transplantation has been attempted in a few humans.

An epiretinal prosthesis (Argus II System from Second Sight Medical Products) has been evaluated in 30 subjects, and after 3 years 29 still had a functioning system with successful return of some visual function in that eye. It has been approved by the FDA. However the cost was high, about $200,000 per QALY.
There is some evidence from a single small RCT that hyperbaric oxygen therapy may stabilize progression of the disease.

A study of 601 patients, randomized to receive vitamin A 15,000 IU per day, vitamin E 400 IU per day, both, or neither, found that vitamin A supplementation slowed progression of disease, while vitamin E supplementation adversely affected disease, based on ERG changes.

A systematic review identified 11 studies with 355 patients treated with mesenchymal stem cell therapy. While early results (mostly from uncontrolled trials) were promising longer term results from randomized trials are needed.
Refer patients to an ophthalmologist if there is a family history of RP or if the patient complains of nyctalopia or flashing lights.
The urgency of the referral depends on the severity of the symptoms. Contacting an ophthalmologist for discussion may aid in appropriate triage.

Typically, patients experience progressive retinal function loss resulting in constriction of the visual field and possible loss of central acuity. Some patients may have slower progression than is typical for the disease. B
Based on calculated actuarial data, patients not treated with vitamin A can expect a 50% functional decline every 7 years compared with every 8 years in treated patients. B
Patients with retinitis pigmentosa are more likely to report stress, depression and suicidal thoughts than those without the disease.
